claims.claim: For dragons to be believed, everything ordinary must match our reality, down to the hero spilling his coffee.
claims.quote: the hero spills his cup of hot coffee

claims.claim: She does not smooth life out for her characters; it is never going to be all pony rides.
claims.quote: everything is always going to be pony rides

claims.claim: She avoids the language that reaches for 'throbbing' anything.
To write any viewpoint she puts the character on like a coat and believes everything they believe for the duration.
claims.quote: put that character on like a coat

claims.claim: Inside any viewpoint, even the villain is wondering what is for dinner.
claims.quote: even the villain is wondering what is for dinner

claims.claim: As Hobb she sprawls in novels and knows it; her Lindholm prose is much leaner.
claims.quote: In a novel, I sprawl, and I know it

claims.claim: The Hobb voice is leisurely, with more emotion and more pausing over what characters think or feel, where Lindholm reports what happened.
claims.quote: writes in a much more leisurely manner

claims.claim: The Hobb name was created to write with a depth of feeling she did not usually indulge.
claims.quote: a depth of feeling that I didn't usually indulge

claims.claim: A story idea belongs immediately and unmistakably to one of the two voices.

claims.feature: story equals how events affect characters
claims.claim: The story is about how events affect the characters, not about the events.
claims.quote: how the events affect the characters

claims.feature: every character main character of own story
claims.claim: Each character, villain included, is written as the main character in his own story.
claims.quote: the main character in his own story

claims.feature: vocabulary as a way of seeing
claims.claim: Characters are differentiated by vocabulary, sentence structure, slang and cadence, because word choice is a way of seeing.
claims.quote: Choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things

claims.claim: How a character reacts to an event reveals more than exposition does.
A believable character is shaped by the world they grew up in, not dropped into it.
claims.quote: The character has to be shaped by the world

claims.claim: In any description she tries to engage as many of the five senses as possible.
claims.quote: engage as many of them as possible

verdicts.trueWording: the hero spills his cup of hot coffee
verdicts.note: helsinkitimes.fi live, HTTP 200, raw HTML fetched and de-tagged. Page: 'if I want you to believe in dragons and magic, then everything else that is mundane and ordinary has to match our reality, and that means there are times when the hero spills his cup of hot coffee, or they miss an airplane'. Quote is an exact substring; every limb (dragons believed / ordinary must match reality / spilled coffee) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't smooth it out ... always pony rides in the sunshine
verdicts.note: Same Helsinki Times paragraph as index 15: 'I don't smooth it out and say that everything is always going to be pony rides in the sunshine. It is the normal ups and downs of life.' Exact substring. The 'for her characters' limb is carried by the following sentence about readers identifying with those characters.

verdicts.trueWording: I try to avoid the language that wants ... his or her "throbbing" whatever
verdicts.note: Exact word-for-word match; the only difference is quote-mark style (the page puts double quotes around "throbbing", the claim uses single). Context is romance-writing diction: 'That's not how I describe a lovely meal, so we're not writing something that's salacious.'

verdicts.trueWording: I really have to put that character on like a coat
verdicts.note: Exact substring. Page continues: 'I am now Kennit. I feel absolutely justified... I have to share his convictions and his righteousness and his fears and his paranoia, and I have to be that character for the time it takes me to write them' — supporting both the believes-what-they-believe and for-the-duration limbs. Minor narrowing: the page frames it as 'when I am writing from a tight third-person point of view' rather than any viewpoint. Independently corroborated on the Writing Excuses transcript ('you put on that character like you'd put on a coat and you wear it').

verdicts.trueWording: even the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight
verdicts.note: ofblog.blogspot.com fetched HTTP 200; page header confirms 'The OF Blog: Robin Hobb Interview', Monday, April 28, 2003 — attribution and date correct. Page: 'Climb into a character, and suddenly even the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight and wishing he hadn't worn these uncomfortable shoes'. Exact substring; the 'inside any viewpoint' limb is 'Climb into a character'.

verdicts.trueWording: In a novel, I sprawl, and I know it
verdicts.note: Exact substring. Both limbs on the page in adjacent answers: 'In a novel, I sprawl, and I know it. Luckily I have incredible editors standing by to yank my chain' and 'Prose as Megan Lindholm is much leaner than prose as Robin Hobb.' Note the sprawl sentence is unqualified by pen name; the Hobb/Lindholm contrast comes from the second answer.

verdicts.trueWording: Robin Hobb writes in a much more leisurely manner
verdicts.note: reactormag.com HTTP 200. Page: 'I think Robin Hobb writes in a much more leisurely manner, with a lot more emotion and a lot more pausing about "This is what the characters think or feel"; and Megan Lindholm writes a lot more like "This is what happened."' Every limb of the claim, including the Lindholm reports-what-happened contrast, is verbatim on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: With the new name she wrote with that depth of feeling
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'was created to' — the page gives the depth of feeling as what she then wrote, not as the stated reason the Hobb name was adopted
verdicts.note: gizmodo.com HTTP 200; the page reproduces the full Inheritance preface, so the source attribution is right. Quote exact: 'I wrote with a depth of feeling that I didn't usually indulge.' But the page's stated purposes for the name change are breaking with the past, the appeal of a 'secret identity', and an agreed 'opportunity for me to break out of my "Megan Lindholm" voice and tell a big compelling story in a very lively way'. The depth of feeling is the sentence that follows as consequence. Restate as effect, not purpose.

verdicts.trueWording: when I get a story idea I can immediately tell which voice
verdicts.note: locusmag.com HTTP 200 (the public excerpts page for the December 2005 issue). Page: 'There is a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice and the Megan Lindholm voice in my writing, so when I get a story idea I can immediately tell which voice is the better fit.' Exact substring; 'immediately' and the two-voices limb are both explicit. The page hedges slightly — 'fairly clean' and 'better fit' against the claim's 'unmistakably' — but the operative content (immediate, unambiguous assignment) is stated. The Inheritance preface says the same harder: 'when I get a story idea, I immediately know if it belongs to Lindholm or Hobb'.

verdicts.trueWording: the story is really about how the events affect the characters
verdicts.note: fantasyhotlist.blogspot.com HTTP 200, page titled 'Pat's Fantasy Hotlist: Robin Hobb Interview'. Page: 'For me, the story is really about how the events affect the characters rather than about the events themselves.' Exact substring, and the 'not about the events' limb is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: let each character be the main character in his own story
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'villain included' — the word villain does not occur anywhere on this page (0 occurrences); its examples are a walk-on barmaid and minor characters written to take a bullet or be the romantic prize
verdicts.note: Quote is an exact substring of 'My technique with characters is to try to let each character be the main character in his own story.' The villain limb is real but belongs to a different source — the OF Blog 2003 interview (index 19's page): 'even the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight... If you put on the villain's skin, you have to love him or at least understand him.' Either drop the villain limb here or cite OF Blog for it.

verdicts.trueWording: it's a choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things
verdicts.note: writingexcuses.com HTTP 200. Quote exact (page has the article: 'it's a choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things'). All four differentiators are on the page: vocabulary (Hobb's farmer/sailor galley-head-deck example), sentence structure and slang (Hobb: 'Even the choice of sentence structure... Some characters speak in longer sentences... The use of slang'), and cadence (host Dan Wells: 'the cadence of their sentences', which Hobb affirms: 'That's exactly it, and just those verbal clues to your reader'); the episode's key-points summary lists 'Attitude, sentence structure, slang, cadence'. Only nuance: 'cadence' is the host's word, ratified by Hobb, not originally hers.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'more than exposition does' — the page makes no comparison to exposition; the word exposition never appears, and no ranking of reaction against telling is stated
verdicts.note: Quote exact, but it occurs only in the transcript's editorial key-points header ('Reaction shots reveal character!'), not in anyone's speech. Hobb's own version is unranked: 'how the person reacts to that is a great way to build character... all of the secondary, the reaction shots of this happens, how did my character react?' The claim's comparative is an addition; state it as 'reaction reveals character' without the versus-exposition ranking.

verdicts.trueWording: the character has to be shaped by the world
verdicts.note: Exact substring of 'Because the character has to be shaped by the world.' Both remaining limbs are on the page: grew-up-in ('What formed you at the most basic level? What sort of a family did you grow up in?... Are you wealthy? Are you poor?') and not-dropped-in ('the character has to be generated by the world. I don't think I could take a 21st century any person and believably insert them into a fantasy'), which also supplies 'believable'.

verdicts.trueWording: in a description of anything, I want to engage as many of them
verdicts.note: lisipieces.com HTTP 200. Page carries it twice, in the reporter's summary and in the raw answer: 'I think it goes back to "show don't tell." We have five senses, and in a description of anything, I want to engage as many of them as possible.' Exact substring; the five-senses and any-description limbs are both explicit.
